Describe the reasons or results of events or actions in spoken or written texts, in work and social contexts.
Present Perfect When Commenting on the Present Results of Something in the Past
You use the Present Perfect to talk about past actions that have a connection to the present.
When you want to comment on the present results of a past action you can use the Present Perfect with verbs like appear, seem and sound.
For example:

It sounds as if you've already decided on the next course of action.
It seems they have completed the report ahead of schedule.
The form of the Present Perfect is:
subject + has/have + past participle
You can use since and yet to introduce the past event.

For example:
  • Since the beginning of their friendship, they have tried all sorts of solutions.
  • Yet, no matter what they try, their prickly problem has remained.
Since there has been a lot of talk of late about sadness and conflict, a book about hugs seems like a perfect subject to read during the holiday season.
How to write a review of a book

When you write a review of a book, you are offering a combination of summary and commentary on what you have read.
You are also trying to persuade the reader.
Book reviews are written in formal language and in paragraphs.
Here are the general elements of a book review:

Introduction

You need to provide basic information about the book:

• Title and the author
  • Publication Information
  • Genre
  • A brief introduction to the book and the review
Body
Provide brief descriptions of the setting and other major characters.
Explain the plot.
How would you describe the writing style?
Are there images or illustrations? How do they connect to the text?
Be careful not to give away important plot details or the ending.

You can write about your own opinions.
Would you recommend it to others? Why or why not?
Conclusion
Briefly conclude by pulling your thoughts together. You may want to say what impression the book left you with, or emphasize what you want your reader to know about it.

These are words you write in a review about a children's book.
treat
something pleasant or amusing that is unusual or unexpected
(noun)
Example: He offers the reader a visual treat with images that leap from the page and his incredible attention to detail.
engenn11le15ob08aud02
prickle
one of usually many stiff, sharp points
(noun)
Example: However, there is one thing that these little hedgehogs can't do and that is hug each other because of their pesky prickles.
engenn11le15ob08aud03
to wrap
to cover something by winding or folding a piece of material around it
(verb)
Example: They have even considered wrapping themselves in tissue paper!
engenn11le15ob08aud04
offering
something that is available for sale or use
(noun)
Example: This children's book is the most recent offering by BFP Publishing.
engenn11le15ob08aud05
Christmas stocking
a long sock used to hold small presents at Christmas
(noun)
Example: It is the perfect book for the holiday season and to slip into a Christmas stocking.
engenn11le15ob08aud06
illustrator
a person who draws pictures for books
(noun)
Example: He is a fantastic illustrator.

Write a 12-14 line dialogue between you and a friend about what he/she needs to include in a book review.
Describe the structure of a book review.
Talk about characters, setting and plot.
Explain to your friend the need to express his opinion.
Suggest that he needs to say if he recommends the book or not.
When completed, read the dialogue aloud to a partner.
